demand_analysis.regime: Bimodal campaign-based: alternates between low-activity days (~50-200 units) and high-consumption campaign days (~5500-8500 units)
demand_analysis.distribution_type: Bimodal (mixed low/high demand states); not well-described by a single unimodal distribution

lead_time_analysis.stability: Moderate — short mean lead time (1.03 days) but high relative variability (CV=0.76); occasional spikes above 3 days observed

safety_lead_time.comparison_action: Increase SAP safety lead time from 0.0 to 1.42 days

narrative: PL3__MCD18380 exhibits a pronounced bimodal demand pattern: roughly 12% of working days are low-activity (~50-200 units) while the remaining 88% are high-consumption campaign days averaging ~6,800 units. The current SAP safety stock of 607 units covers less than 0.1 days of average demand, providing virtually no buffer against the observed lead time variability (CV=0.76). An (s,Q) continuous-review policy with ROP=16,772 and Q=5,111 is recommended, which respects the 14,040-unit storage cap while delivering a projected 81% reduction in total annual inventory costs.
warnings: Storage capacity is binding: safety_stock (8928) + order_quantity (5111) = 14039, which equals max_storage_units (14039.853). Zero practical buffer remains.
Order quantity was capped from unconstrained EOQ (5490) to 5111 due to storage capacity constraint.
Bimodal demand structure: standard safety stock formula may underestimate tail risk on campaign days. Quarterly policy review recommended.
Lead time CV=0.76 indicates moderate-to-high supplier variability; reducing lead time sigma would allow meaningful safety stock reduction.

research_insights.selection_rationale: The (s,Q) model is appropriate for this material because: (1) demand is high-volume with daily replenishment monitoring feasible; (2) lead times are short (mean ~1 day) enabling responsive triggering; (3) the bimodal demand structure benefits from a fixed reorder point that captures both low and high-demand regimes; (4) the MOQ constraint aligns naturally with a fixed order quantity Q rather than variable order-up-to policies.
research_insights.boundary_risk: The storage capacity constraint (14,039.853 units) binds exactly at safety_stock + order_quantity = 14,039 units. This leaves virtually no headroom. If demand spikes coincide with a delayed replenishment, available storage may prevent placing a full order. Management should explore a 5-10% storage capacity increase to decouple the safety stock and order quantity decisions.
research_insights.escalation_flag: Capacity is critically tight. Any upward revision to safety stock (e.g., from demand plan changes or improved service level target) will require either a storage expansion or a reduction in order quantity below EOQ-optimal levels. This trade-off should be escalated to supply chain management and site logistics.
